newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Thousands join Church march in Serbia.
newsitem.headline: Thousands join Church march in Serbia.

text.p: Thousands of people filed solemnly through Belgrade on Monday in a march called by the powerful Serbian Orthodox church, which is now siding with demonstrators in their protests against election fraud.

Witnesses said the march was the biggest since half a million people turned out on Orthodox New Year's Eve two weeks ago. It showed support still ran strong for the pro-democracy movement after more than two months of protests.

Patriarch Pavle, head of the Church who is in his 80s, led the procession, estimated at up to 200,000-strong at its peak, through sunny but freezing early morning streets on the holy day of Saint Sava.
The patriarch, flanked by about 20 chanting priests, walked three km (two miles) to celebrate mass at the Temple of Saint Sava, patron saint of educators.
It was the first daytime march in Belgrade since a ban was imposed following clashes between opposition and pro-government demonstrators on December 24.

The march was held on the day that an opposition municipal council was due to be sworn in for Nis, Serbia's second biggest city and one of 14 where opposition victories in November were annulled. The government later ordered the opposition win in Nis to be reinstated.
Police made way for the patriarch's procession by withdrawing a cordon blocking student demonstrators who had held a non-stop rally for eight days in a test of will with the authorities.

Later on Monday, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Igor Ivanov was due to meet Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic in a bid to help break the standoff over the government's annulment of the opposition victories.

Western diplomats said Ivanov's visit came as a surprise. But they were cautious about suggesting it could lead to a breakthrough in the impasse that has prompted daily protests posing the biggest threat to Milosevic in 10 years in power.
"It was a surprise that he (Ivanov) showed up and any mediation might be helpful," one diplomat said.
The diplomat pointed out that the Russians, who have close ties with the Serbian leadership, had been promoting dialogue between the two sides.
The Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition maintains its election victories, which have been verified by the West, are not negotiable.
After police had withdrawn their cordon in Belgrade, 50,000 students and their supporters swept triumphantly through the city in a boisterous, whistle-blowing march.
"This is our great victory," said student Djordje Todorovic. "I feel glorious and victorious."
There were shouts of "Let's go for a walk" and "Let's go to Dedinje" -- a reference to the Belgrade neighbourhood where Milosevic lives.
At the head of one column, marchers carried two Serbian flags, a statue of Jesus Christ and a candle.
The students later linked up with the church procession and student organisers acted as orderlies, controlling the crowd while traffic police looked on.
The Orthodox Church, which backed Serb nationalist war aims during the Yugoslav conflict, stayed silent for weeks while pro-democracy protests swept Serbia.
But Patriarch Pavle blessed student protesters at a rally last week and priests have frequently attended the demonstrations.
The church's involvement stepped up the pressure on Milosevic to acknowledge the victories by Zajedno.
The opposition wins were annulled because of alleged irregularities but Milosevic has been under strong pressure from the West to reinstate them.
